chapter_theme: The base (கயமை): their nature is not changed by age, learning or wealth. They give only under force, remember insults and forget kindnesses, speak ill of others to their faces, and hold their wealth without softening.
structure_note: Almost every quatrain sets the base against the worthy and carries the point with an image from nature or work: the hollow எருவை (351), the frog in the pond (352), the chisel (355), the boar's tusks (358), the lotus leaf (359) and the dry netti reed (360). 359 names no base person, and the link to the chapter is Mudaliar's.

351.reading: The fully wise restrain and guard themselves even when young in years, while the petty-minded grow more practised in wrongdoing the older they get and, like the எருவை, never lose their hollowness.
351.nuance: Age is set aside as a cause: wisdom doesn't wait for years, and years don't cure folly. Mudaliar gives two senses for both எருவை and போத்து: a reed that never fills its hollow, or a kite that never sheds its faults. Shanmuganar takes the kite and the faults, and Pope the hollow reed.

352.reading: Frogs that live in a rich, large pond never rid themselves of their slime; in the same way, those without fine discernment rarely gain the power to examine what they read, even after studying flawless, excellent books.
352.nuance: What is missing is not learning but நுணுக்கம், a subtlety that study doesn't supply. The pond's abundance matches the excellence of the books: neither reaches what is already in the creature. Shanmuganar's commentary on this quatrain appears under 351.

353.reading: Lord of the good land of clustered hills: it is hard even to speak of a man's virtues when he isn't present, so what are the tongues of petty people made of, that they stand at his side and proclaim his faults until his virtues are spoiled?
353.nuance: Both commentators read கண் இன்று as 'not before his eyes', and Mudaliar rejects splitting it as கண் நின்று. The contrast is then between a decent reluctance to praise someone even behind his back and the brazenness of faulting him beside him. Pope takes the other split and has the praise spoken to the man's face.

354.reading: Household women do not know how to dress up their womanliness the way their maids do it for them; the other kind, like a fresh flood, put their charms on show themselves, think highly of themselves, and then pass on.
354.nuance: In a chapter on the base the verse works as a figure, and Mudaliar names it பிறிது மொழிதல்: the wise don't praise themselves, and fools vaunt themselves to extract wealth. The verse itself speaks only of the two kinds of women.

positions.position: இறப்பர் means the courtesans leave a man once they have taken all his wealth; the verse is an allegory of fools who praise themselves to get money.
இறப்பர் means they overstep all bounds, rating themselves highly; he reads the verse as a contrast between the women themselves.

355.reading: The base are like a chisel that won't cut in, even set on a tender shoot, unless someone strikes it: they do nothing at all for the kind, and anything at all for those who treat them harshly.
355.nuance: A tender shoot is the softest thing a chisel could meet, so the image says the base yield to nothing gentle. Mudaliar lets அளிநீரார் mean either the compassionate or those whose state calls for pity.

356.reading: The hill-dweller thinks of the wealth of his hills and the farmer of the field that yielded; the worthy think of a good someone did them, while the base dwell on the time someone abused them.
356.nuance: The first two figures set up the rule that each mind returns to what it values; the last two say what the worthy and the base value. Mudaliar notes the verse calls the base man கயம், a neuter noun, to show how low he is.

357.reading: The worthy bear a hundred faults, coming one after another, from someone who once did them a kindness; for the base, if one thing goes wrong after seven hundred kindnesses, all seven hundred turn into harm.
357.nuance: Mudaliar takes the hundred and the seven hundred as standing for 'many' and 'very many'. The asymmetry is the point: for one kind of person a single kindness outweighs a hundred wrongs, and for the other a single wrong cancels seven hundred kindnesses.

358.reading: What those of good family do even when weakened by want, the utterly foolish don't do even at the height of their fortune; bright-eyed one, fit a boar's tusks with diamond rings and it still won't become an angry war elephant.
358.nuance: The verse doesn't name the deeds. Pope supplies liberality, and Mudaliar says only 'good deeds'. The base are called முழுமக்கள், which Mudaliar glosses as fools, so the lack here is of sense as well as of birth.

359.reading: Many people thought 'today we'll have it, right now, or in a little while', rejoiced as they said so to others, and then, their hopes overturned, perished like lotus leaves.
359.nuance: The verse doesn't say what they expected, and names no base person. Mudaliar supplies both: they waited to become rich without doing good, and withered like the lotus leaf that flourishes and dies where it stands. Shanmuganar's commentary for this quatrain is missing.

360.reading: Though it is born in water and is green, the netti reed has no moisture in its pith; in the same way the world holds men who stay hard as great rock slabs even while living in full, great wealth.
360.nuance: The image is exact: the plant lives in water and holds none, as these men live among plenty and give none. Mudaliar's gloss on the rock is that it never softens (இளகுதல்).

links.note: Both say study does not change what a person is: 823 says the unworthy rarely become good at heart however many good books they learn, and 352 says those without fine discernment never gain it from flawless books.

184 ranks harsh words to a man's face above careless words behind his back. 353 doesn't let face-to-face speech off: the base are shameless precisely because they list a man's faults standing beside him.
On Mudaliar's reading of 354 as a figure, both make self-display the mark of the small: 978 says smallness adorns itself in self-admiration, and 354's wantons adorn and vaunt themselves.
Both say the base give only to force: 1077's base won't shake their wet hands except for those who would break their jaws, and 355's chisel only moves when struck.
1078's sugar-cane yields only when crushed, and 355's chisel cuts only when struck: two tools of labour for the same claim about the base.
108 tells one to keep a good done in mind and forget the bad that very day. 356 says the worthy do exactly this and the base do the reverse, dwelling on abuse.

Both make one kindness outweigh great injury: in 109 a wrong as painful as killing vanishes at the thought of one good, and in 357 the worthy bear a hundred faults for one kindness. 357 adds the base, for whom the scale runs the other way.
955 says an old family doesn't part from its nature even when its means shrink, and 358 says the well-born do in poverty what the base won't do in wealth.
Both mock plans made without regard to life's shortness: 337's unwise think crores of thoughts without knowing they'll live a moment more, and 359's dreamers say 'today, now, soon' and perish.

Both picture people who have the means of feeling and none of the feeling: 576's men have eyes but no kind regard and are like trees in the soil, and 360's rich live in wealth but stay dry as the netti's pith.

source_issues: 351: Shanmuganar's field also contains the text of 352 and his commentary on it, and 352 has no Shanmuganar commentary aligned.
353: the Tamil reads கா஢தால், a garbled character; Mudaliar's gloss அரிது gives அரிதால்.
356: Shanmuganar's field also contains the text and his commentary for 357 and 358 and the text of 359; 357 and 358 have no Shanmuganar commentary aligned, and none exists for 359.
360: Shanmuganar's field ends with the heading of the next chapter.
